text:
Kathāsaritsāgara | [Initial Wave 100]

He offered me great flesh <note>original: "mahāmāṃsa," referring to human flesh</note> for my satisfaction; I ate it immediately, and being satisfied, the one craving human flesh said to me, "Ask for no other boon." When I could not endure the time any longer, I sliced off my own flesh, which brings pleasure, and gave it to him. The <term>Yogeśvara</term> <gloss>Lord of Yoga/Master of Yogis</gloss> was pleased with me for that. 49-50

Then he said to me, "Friend, I am now satisfied with your firm resolve. Therefore, brave one, be whole-bodied as before, and choose from me your desired boon." When he said this, I replied to him at that very moment, "Lord, take me to that place where my master, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term>, resides; I desire no other boon beyond this." 51-52

Having heard this, the Lord of the <term>Vetālas</term> <gloss>vampire-like spirits</gloss> said to me, "Then climb upon my flesh-covered back; I shall quickly take you to that lord of yours in the sky." Upon his saying this, I agreed, saying, "So be it," and I climbed upon his shoulders. Then, having entered a ghost-body, he carried me and set out through the path of the sky. 53-54

Having brought me here, he saw you, lowered me from the sky along the way, and through this noble <term>Vetāla</term>, I was brought to the base of your feet, O Lord. Having met you, my master, I have reached my goal, my task completed. This is the great story of my separation, O bestower of honor, after I was released from the serpent-noose. 55-56

Having heard the account of the separation from his minister, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term>, while traveling on the road to <term>Ujjayinī</term> for the sake of his beloved, was filled with joy. That prince, having met a few of his followers who had strayed but then returned, and having obtained all possible success, rejoiced. 57-58

This is the thirty-second wave in the <term>Śaśāṅkavatī</term> <gloss>Moon-like/Having Moon-like beauty</gloss> book of the Kathāsaritsāgara, composed by the great poet, the illustrious <term>Somadeva Bhaṭṭa</term>.

The Thirty-Third Wave.

Salutation to the conqueror of obstacles, upon whose knee the necklace of stars revolves as he dances in the nights, like the pots on a water-wheel. 1

Then, at the end of the story, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term> arose from the middle of the road, having found <term>Vikramakesarī</term> filled with joy. 2

Accompanied by <term>Guṇākara</term>, <term>Vimalabuddhi</term>, the story-teller <term>Vicitraka</term>, and the valorous <term>Bhīmaparākrama</term>, along with <term>Pracaṇḍaśakti</term> and the learned Brahmin <term>Śrutadhi</term>, he searched for the remaining companions who had been separated by the curse. 3-4

Having reached the road to <term>Ujjayinī</term> to seek <term>Śaśāṅkavatī</term> before anyone else, he set out again, the eighth among them. 5

Gradually, he reached a forest, fearful with its dried-up riverbeds and sands scorched by the heat of the fierce sun. 6

Walking through it, the prince said to those ministers, "Look, how impassable and frightening this forest is. 7

It is a place devoid of paths, without people, and lacking any shelter; it is as if the desert mirages have become the rising flames of a fire. 8

With its dry, disheveled vegetation, its rustling dried grass, and its thorns that make the hair stand on end with the fear of lions, tigers, and other beasts, 9

it seems to be weeping with its deer that desire water at the edges of its dried-up ponds. Therefore, we must cross this vast, difficult forest quickly." 10

Having said this, Prince <term>Mṛgāṅkadatta</term>, along with his ministers who were afflicted by hunger and thirst, quickly crossed that forest. 11

In front, he saw a very large lake with clear, cool water, like the liquid essence of the moon melted by the heat of the sun. 12

<note>A decorative floral ornament marks the end of the chapter.</note>

<summary>A minister recounts how he reached Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta by the help of a Vetāla, and the prince subsequently sets out with his reunited companions through a desert forest to find his beloved.</summary>
<keywords>Mṛgāṅkadatta, Vikramakesarī, Vetāla, Ujjayinī, Śaśāṅkavatī, quest, forest, travel</keywords>
